To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in cold cities, cold temperatures increase CVD deaths, whereas high temperatures increase CVD and MI deaths; that the effect of cold days persists for days, whereas for hot days, it is restricted to the day before or the day of the event; that the effect for CVD deaths is larger than for MI deaths; that in cold cities the effect of cold-day temperatures persists for days, but there is no clear pattern for hot days; and that hot temperatures increase MI deaths in hot cities.

cold weather is a risk factor for CVD deaths and MI, but not for pneumonia deaths; hot weather is a risk for MI and chronic bronchitis, but not for all CVD and pneumonia deaths; and hot weather has some effect on CVD deaths in cold cities, but no effect in warm cities.
cold temperatures increase cardiovascular deaths, especially in cold cities, whereas hot temperatures are more important in hot cities, and the effects of cold and hot temperatures persist for days.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the cold-day effect is a major contributor to excess CVD and respiratory deaths, whereas the hot-day effect is less important, but it may be more important than we have previously thought for MI and chronic pulmonary disease deaths.
the effect of weather is not the same everywhere.
the effect of hot temperatures on respiratory deaths is restricted to hot cities and the effect of cold days on CVD and pneumonia deaths is restricted to cold cities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effect of temperature on mortality is not uniform and depends on the type of death, the season, and the location.
the effect of temperature varies with location, and that there is substantial spatial heterogeneity of both the effect of temperature and the weather conditions that cause the effect.
the effect of temperature on CVD deaths is different in hot and cold cities, with hot cities being more vulnerable to hot temperatures and cold cities being more vulnerable for cold temperatures.
